units: the frame that carries the roof may be of timber or of metal
this frame passes the weight of the roof into the load-bearing walls
slim pieces of wood are nailed across it to take the covering
the covering described is a dark stone split into flat sheets
this covering lets the space beneath the roof breathe
a channel set at the foot of the slope gathers rainwater
this water is then sent into a downpipe
an opening cut into the slope lights and airs the storey under the roof
this opening weakens the watertightness if it is poorly fitted
a specialist tradesman checks the whole of it before the wet months
text: Every part of a roof does a job of its own. The frame beneath, built of timber or of steel, holds the whole thing up and passes its weight down into the load-bearing walls. Across that frame run the battens, slim strips of wood nailed at intervals, and the covering hangs on them. Slate, a dark stone that splits into flat even sheets, keeps the rain out while the space underneath goes on breathing. Along the foot of each slope sits a gutter, gathering what runs off and feeding it into a downpipe, so that the walls are never left soaking. Higher up, a dormer cuts through the slope to bring light and air into the roof space; its surround asks for careful fitting, since any opening breaks the run of the covering. A roofer who knows the trade goes over every one of these before the wet months.

units: workmen were taking up a damaged floor at the top of an empty house
a workman's tool struck something hard beneath a board
an old timber covered in notches was uncovered
the person in charge of the site stopped the work
a restoration specialist came to look at the find the next day
she identified marks cut by the builder who first raised it
these marks showed in what order the structure was to be put together
the owner gave up the idea of replacing the structure
he chose to have it strengthened instead
the timber is left on show and protected by a pale coating
text: Work had begun with the taking up of a rotten floor, on the top storey of a village house that had stood empty through two winters. Lifting the third board, the labourer felt his bar jar against something solid. He brushed the dust aside and freed an old beam, blackened with age, its hidden face scored with a run of even notches. The foreman stopped everything. A building conservator came out the following morning, ran her palm along the grain and recognised jointing marks cut by the carpenter who first raised the roof. Each piece, she said, had been lettered before it went up, so that the frame could be assembled in its proper order, like the words of a sentence taken apart. Told of it at the weekend, the owner dropped the plan to replace the frame and asked instead that it be strengthened. The beam still shows in the ceiling, under a pale wax.

units: the moisture of the wall must be checked before a light partition goes up
a damp background stops the covering from holding
the skim comes away in flakes at the first heating if the background is wet
the setting-out line is marked with a taut string
a floor track out of level throws out every upright and ripples the finish
the bonding compound is mixed in small amounts because it sets quickly
a screw driven too deep spoils the surface and weakens the board's hold
laying jointing tape on a wet background makes it swell and then crack
a gap left at the foot of the partition protects it from rising damp
text: Before a light partition goes up, take a moisture reading of the wall behind it, for plaster will not grip a damp background and the skim comes away in flakes the moment the heating goes on. Snap the setting-out line onto the floor with a chalked string, then fix the floor track, because a track laid off the level hands its error to every upright and the finished face will ripple. Mix the bonding compound a little at a time, since it stiffens fast and a big batch ends up thrown away. Drive each screw home without breaking through the paper, or the head tears the facing and the board loses its hold. Let the work dry before skimming, as tape bedded over a wet joint swells and splits in the end. Leave a small gap along the foot of the partition too, or the least rise of damp will stain it.

units: neighbours in a low-lying area had flooded cellars after heavy rain
the trouble had lasted since the end of summer
a study was ordered by the local authority
the drainage network had been planned for ground that soaked up water
yards covered over with concrete have done away with that soaking up
the water reached the doorways of the houses and ran under the doors
the paths will be laid with a gravelly material that lets water through
channels running along the walls will take the water to a basin dug further off
the money comes from a grant and from a payment by the owners
a first stretch will be finished before the wet season
text: Since the end of summer, people living in a low-lying district have reported flooded cellars after every heavy shower. A study ordered by the local authority found that the drainage network, laid out when the ground still soaked up rain, could no longer cope once the yards had been concreted over. Nothing was taken in any more, so the water slid towards the thresholds and worked its way under the doors. The technical department have settled on an answer in two parts. The paths are to be lifted and laid again with loose gravel, which lets the rain sink away instead of throwing it back at the buildings. Shallow channels will then follow the exposed walls and carry the flow into a holding basin dug well clear of the houses. A grant to the authority covers most of the cost, the owners paying the rest. A first stretch is due before the rains.

units: two dwellings look at one another from the two sides of a narrow street
they share no feature at all
the house on the left has a pale covering on its walls
its openings are closed by painted wooden panels
above each opening on the left runs a visible oak beam
the house on the right has stone walls left bare
its openings are narrower and capped by a beam of hard stone
it is guarded by metal slats that slide instead of hinged panels
the first gives a sense of welcome, the second a sense of closing off
the entrance steps differ too, one of wood hollowed by use, the other a heavy slab
text: Two houses stand facing one another from either side of a narrow street, and they have nothing whatever in common. The one on the left shows a front rendered in pale lime wash, its tall windows shut behind wooden shutters painted grey. Over every opening a length of oak carries the wall above, barely curved, softening the flat face of the render. The one on the right answers with bare stone, the joints raked out, and its windows are narrower, each capped by a thick granite beam. No shutter swings there: metal slats instead run down in a rebate cut for them. The first looks welcoming, a little worn by the weather, while the second seems shut, heavy, cut to stand up to the wind. Even the two doorsteps part company, one of wood hollowed by feet, the other a cold slab of stone.

units: the writer holds that buildings are pulled down too easily instead of being put right
his first reproach bears on the waste of material still fit for use
careful dismantling costs more than quick destruction
his second reproach concerns the loss of the hand trades
these skills die out along with the places that taught them
his third reproach aims at the disappointing comfort of new building
new building suffers heat in the warm season and draughts in the cold one
the bill falls on whoever lives in the dwelling
his fourth reproach is that what the occupants feel for the place counts for nothing
he does not ask that everything be kept but wants proof that repair was impossible
text: Let us be blunt: we knock buildings down far too readily and mend them far too rarely. First reproach, the waste of good material. A sound roof frame, tiles fit to go back up, an oak staircase, all of it goes in the skip because careful stripping out costs more than an afternoon with a machine. Second reproach, the hollowing out of the hand trades. Who can still repoint in lime, straighten a sagging beam, split a slate without shattering it? Those skills die with the workshops that passed them on. Third reproach, the promised comfort never turns up: the freshly built one bakes in the warm months, whistles in the cold ones, and whoever lives there pays for it. Fourth reproach, what people feel for the place they have lived in weighs nothing in the decision. I do not argue for keeping everything, only for proof that no serious repair was open to us.

units: the woman spoken of grew up beside a place where stone was got out of the ground
her father worked there cutting stone out of the rock
she watched the blocks being split before doing it herself
she took up training in a workshop that put old buildings right
her first job of note was replacing a worn doorstep
she then took on harder work such as a split beam and a vault to rebuild
she set up her own workshop about ten years after she began
she employs two workers
she now teaches beginners, several of whom had never worked with their hands
she holds that this material calls for patience
text: A quarryman's daughter, the stonemason grew up beside a limestone working, watching blocks split long before she held a chisel herself. She went on to take up an apprenticeship in a yard given over to restoration work, learning to read the bed of the stone, and her first job of any weight was the worn doorstep of an old wayside inn. Heavier work followed soon enough: a cracked beam to take out and match, a vault to set back stone by stone. Ten winters or so after she began she opened a yard of her own, where two masons now work alongside her from one week to the next. Lately she gives part of each week to apprentices drawn from all sorts of backgrounds, several of whom had never handled a tool. Stone, she says, forgives impatience badly, and what she really teaches is how to slow the hand.

units: the visitor leaves this restored building with a feeling of being shut in
this feeling comes from choices of construction rather than from a quarrel over taste
an insulating skin was added in front of the old walls
this addition has sunk the windows into a deep recess
the view towards the outside is now blocked
a stretched ceiling hides the timber structure that used to be in sight
this hiding makes the place lose the size it seemed to have
the floor of gravel was replaced by a smooth surface
this surface throws the sound back and makes the noise hard to bear
the critic approves of keeping the entrance step worn by passing feet
text: You come out of this restored hall with a feeling of being shut in, and the fault lies less with taste than with the way the work was done. The designers lined the old walls with an unbroken insulating skin, so that the windows have sunk into deep throats and the eye is stopped short of the outside. The roof frame, once readable from one end of the building to the other, has gone behind a stretched ceiling, and with it goes the height that made the room feel generous. The floor of rolled gravel, replaced now by a smooth screed, throws voices back off the bare surfaces and turns a murmur into a din. One decision alone consoles: the entrance step has been kept, hollowed by generations of feet, a reminder that the place was in daily use long before anyone thought to smarten it up.

units: the writer addresses his neighbour in writing
he speaks of the channel for gathering water fixed along the shared wall
this channel has been overflowing since the recent rain
the water is spoiling the covering of the wall and laying the mortar bare
an inspection showed a blockage made of leaves and an empty nest
a fixing bracket has given way and tipped part of the channel
the writer offers to clear the channel himself shortly
he offers to change the broken brackets and put the fall right
he suggests fitting a guard so that the trouble does not come back
he asks his neighbour to agree to these proposals
text: Dear neighbour, I am writing to you about the gutter that runs along the wall our two houses share. Since last week's downpours it has spilled over halfway down its length, and the water is eating into the render, which has begun to crumble and show the mortar behind. I put a ladder up: the channel is choked with packed leaves and an abandoned nest, and one bracket has given way, so that stretch of it now tilts backwards. May I suggest three things to you. A thorough clearing out first, which I can do myself before the week is out. Then fresh brackets in place of the broken ones, which cost very little, with the fall put right towards the downpipe. Lastly a guard over the mouth of the channel, so that none of this happens again. Do let me know whether that arrangement suits you.

units: the text compares building with a timber structure and building in concrete
this comparison comes up when a client looks at two priced offers
timber allows quick putting together because the parts are made up beforehand
its lightness allows shallower foundations
timber fears water and calls for wide roof overhangs
the points where timber meets the ground need particular watching
concrete stores heat and softens swings of temperature
it also cuts down noise from outside
its making has a high cost for the environment and its drying lengthens the work
the usual answer joins a concrete base to a timber structure
text: Should one build in timber frame or in concrete? The question comes up as soon as a client sets two tenders side by side. What does timber offer? Quick erection, parts made up beforehand in the workshop, a tidy site, and a light structure that can sit on shallower foundations. What is held against it? Its dislike of water, which calls for generous roof overhangs and steady watchfulness wherever the timber comes near the ground. What does concrete offer? A mass that takes up heat, evens out swings of temperature and deadens the noise of the street. What is held against concrete? A heavy cost in the making, and a programme stretched out by the drying. So which should be chosen? In practice the two are married, a solid base carrying a light frame, and that serves the building better than a clean choice either way.
